paras: The threatened lynching of William Henry Harrison took place in Belleville, New Jersey, on the night of August 4, 1888, when a crowd threatened to lynch Harrison, a Black laborer, after his arrest for the fatal stabbing of William Barnett. Harrison was not harmed; he was committed to the jail in Newark, and a coroner's jury charged him with murder.

The quarrel began in Andrew Reinhard's beer shop on Belleville's main street, where Barnett, 30, was discussing politics when Harrison, about 48, made a remark the Tribune called "derogatory to Irishmen." Barnett answered that his father was Irish, the two men came to blows, and Reinhard put them out through opposite doors.

The men met again in a lane leading to the Passaic bridge and fought until they reached the bridge tender's house, where witnesses saw Harrison crowd Barnett onto the porch and then walk away. Barnett fell with blood pouring from his neck and died before a doctor arrived; the wound had severed the jugular vein.

Justice of the Peace Sandford and a constable found Harrison crossing the street and took him into custody. According to the New-York Tribune, "a crowd soon gathered and threats were made to lynch the prisoner," who kept a "cool demeanor." In a statement at Sandford's court, Harrison said Barnett had tripped him and that he had only choked Barnett, adding, "I never carry a knife."

Harrison was committed to the Newark jail for murder the next day. On August 7 a coroner's inquest returned a verdict charging him with Barnett's murder. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Only the New-York Tribune mentioned the lynch threat, in a single sentence under the headline "Fatally Stabbed by a Negro." The Sun headed its shorter account "Murder Due to Political Talk," described Harrison as "a pretty hard man" who had "been in trouble many times," and called Barnett "popular and inoffensive when sober." The Sun also noted that Harrison had been named for President William Henry Harrison, a detail a South Carolina paper turned into the headline "Not Benjy's Grandpa" over a two-line wire item on the inquest. A Connecticut paper ran the same inquest item among its condensed dispatches, giving the dead man's name as "Barrett."

bases: A crowd gathered after Harrison's arrest for a fatal stabbing and threatened to lynch him while he was held by a justice of the peace; no attack on him is reported (A1).
The only report of mob action is the Tribune's line that a crowd made threats to lynch Harrison; he was not harmed and was committed to the Newark jail, so no one was killed by a mob (A1, A2).
The stabbing, arrest and inquest are reported by four papers (A1, A2, A3, A4), but the lynch threat appears only in the New-York Tribune (A1); the Sun's account does not mention it (A2).

accounts.label: Witnesses from the beer shop (Tribune narrative)
accounts.gist: After a renewed fight in the street, Harrison crowded Barnett onto the bridge tender's porch and walked off; Barnett fell with blood gushing from a deep neck wound that severed the jugular vein.

accounts.label: Harrison's statement before Justice Sandford
accounts.gist: Barnett tripped him and was the stronger man; Harrison said he only choked Barnett at the bridge tender's stoop and had no razor or knife.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: The inquest returned a verdict charging Harrison with Barnett's murder.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined the story 'FATALLY STABBED BY A NEGRO' but gave Harrison's own statement at length and reported the lynch threats in one sentence without comment.

The Sun framed it as 'MURDER DUE TO POLITICAL TALK', called Harrison 'a negro' with a reputation as 'a pretty hard man', called Barnett 'popular and inoffensive when sober', and noted Harrison was named for President Harrison.
Brief wire items on the inquest ran in Connecticut and South Carolina, the latter under the joke headline 'Not Benjy's Grandpa.'
